lines.watchItem: Accelerator demand keeps running ahead of what the chain can ship, and the largest cloud spenders raised 2026 budgets again this cycle. Wafer-start planning across leading-edge nodes carries the exposure if that spending pace turns.

Advanced packaging is still the gate on how much accelerator revenue can actually ship, with lead times of roughly 52 to 78 weeks and bookings running into 2027. The capacity ramp toward about 125,000 to 130,000 wafers a month narrows the gap but does not close it this year.

Three clients take more than 85% of advanced-packaging output, with one at roughly 60% and another at about 11% that it splits between server processors and accelerators. Any single order cut leaves scarce capacity that is hard to refill quickly.

Stacked memory now caps accelerator output alongside packaging: 2026 output is fully committed, 2027 is largely pre-booked, and one supplier holds about 56% of that market. Packaging relief alone would not lift shipments while memory stays the tighter of the two limits.

The leading-node customer base is broadening away from a single dominant accelerator vendor: custom AI chips are forecast to grow 44.6% this year against 16.1% for merchant accelerators, and AMD is converting gigawatt-scale commitments into volume. Two design houses account for roughly 95% of the custom-chip co-design work, so the alternative demand is itself concentrated.

Pricing across the chain stays firm: foundry gross margin reached 67.7% with full-year revenue growth guidance lifted above 40%, and the lead accelerator vendor holds a 75% gross margin. Rack component costs are climbing 2% to 3% a week on memory scarcity, so the pressure point shifts to who absorbs that input inflation.

A second-source foundry track is gaining visible traction: Intel Foundry revenue rose 31% year over year with a named external customer and new node capacity in Ireland, while one large model developer is in early talks with Samsung about a 2-nanometer custom chip. These are early signals rather than volume shifts.

China access reopened only on paper: licensing moved to case-by-case review with a cap and a 25% tariff, yet shipments remain trivial and China data-center revenue halved year over year. Smuggling prosecutions and a shortened customer whitelist tighten the informal route at the same time.
